account:
Today I have been keeping my appointments: office business this morning, the ten o'clock mill inspection, lunch at home, and now council letters at one. At the mill stall I found 128 hay bales offered at two emeralds each. That establishes stock on hand, not its quality or the adequacy of the town's supply. I still have tea with the neighbour at the east-bank dockside cottage at three and an office return at four thirty.

The unusual business is the persistent talk of a bridge or port change at the bakery. Several townsfolk repeat almost identical fragments without explaining a proposal, its purpose, or who authorized it. Townsfolk 11 associated the baker, Freight and the neighbour with the bakery and reported seeing the baker carrying a sack of bread. That is a report, not something I witnessed, and carrying bread is ordinary work for the baker. I have not established that these people are arranging any change together.

Yesterday the innkeeper denied originating the rumor and pointed only to Townsfolk 03. The builder reported a passable bridge without confirmed defects and relayed Freight's report of sound roads and an uneventful ferry crossing. The secretary likewise has no verified news of a change. I authorized only a visual survey, not repairs or alterations; the survey fee and the builder's and secretary's book expenses have been recorded separately.

My present suspicion is that discussion about transport or trade is circulating without reaching me in any definite form, but repeated rumor could also account for it. I do not yet know its purpose or whether there is an actual plan. The secretary is nearby carrying a book, the builder is beside me, and the baker is at the market stall. I should keep the council-letters appointment, hear any concrete report, and seek firsthand particulars rather than treat these fragments as proof.
